title: Dad, Look!
author: Wisdom From Dad
summary: Writing under the pen name "John" for Wisdom From Dad, the author uses his own failed childhood piano lessons, four years of rigid structure that never once let him "jam" the way he actually wanted to play, as a parable for a lesson he says he then repeated with his own children. His diagnosis is that both Miss Audrey and his parents mistook fundamentals for the whole of teaching, missing that a child's genuine interest (in his case, garage-band rock over metronomes and scales) is the actual entry point that makes discipline bearable. He layers in Dale Carnegie's account of becoming a fascinating conversationalist purely by giving full attention to another person's interests, Marcus Aurelius's warning that time is finite and never returns, and John Maxwell's "30-Second Rule" (open every conversation with something encouraging) as practical tools for a father trying to actually notice his children rather than manage them. The piece closes with a reframed definition of the job: children are not projects to be optimized but people to be discovered, and fathers don't need to be perfect, only attentive.
points: Uses a personal account of quitting piano lessons at age ten, because rigid fundamentals never connected to his actual interest in music, as a parable for missing what a child is genuinely trying to communicate.

Applies Dale Carnegie's anecdote about becoming 'a fascinating conversationalist' purely by giving full attention to someone else's interests, arguing children similarly need to be the subject of interest, not merely accommodated.

Introduces John Maxwell's '30-Second Rule' (say something encouraging within the first thirty seconds of any conversation) as a concrete, repeatable practice for connecting with children specifically.

Reframes the parenting task explicitly: 'Our children are not projects; they are people. Our job isn't to manufacture their future, it's to pay enough attention to discover the person who is already there.'
quotes: Why is it that no one picked up on the fact that I loved playing the piano? I just hated the structured practice. I was overwhelmed, frustrated and bored.
The fundamentals matter, but they only matter if we can connect them to the person we're teaching. My parents and good ole Miss Audrey missed this, and so did I.
Carnegie understood something I wish I had understood as a father: People don't need us to be interested in everything they're interested in. They need us to be interested in them.
Within the first thirty seconds of a conversation, say something encouraging to the other person. That's it. It works equally well between parent and child.
Our children are not projects; they are people. Our job isn't to manufacture their future, it's to pay enough attention to discover the person who is already there.
